sections.b: The letter of the church of Rome to Corinth (about the end of the first century) was written because the Corinthians had removed elders who "served the flock of Christ without blame" (1 Clement 44:3-6). Clement calls the same men holders of "the office of overseer" (44:4) and "elders" (44:5), which led Lightfoot to judge the two words synonyms in the letter, as in Acts 20:17 and 20:28 and Titus 1:5-7. Whether that holds for the whole church of the time, the churches answer differently: see the cards at Philippians 1:1, Acts 20:28 and Titus 1:5-7. He tells the rebels to "submit to the elders" (57:1) and asks their leaders to leave so that Christ's flock may "live in peace with the elders who have been appointed" (54:2). The letter also says the elders were appointed by the apostles or later "by other respected men with the whole church agreeing" (44:3).

1 Clement says the apostles appointed their first converts "overseers and deacons for those who would later believe" (1 Clement 42:4), the pair of Philippians 1:1. To show that this was "nothing new," it quotes a form of Isaiah 60:17 that names "their deacons in faith" (42:5), though neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Isaiah mentions deacons; Lightfoot calls the change a "misquotation."

sections.h: 1 Clement: the apostles sent by Christ
sections.b: "The apostles were given the good news for us by the Lord Jesus Christ. Jesus the Christ was sent out from God" (1 Clement 42:1). The Roman letter describes the apostles going out "with the full certainty the Holy Spirit gives" after the resurrection, preaching "from region to region and city to city," testing their first converts by the Spirit and appointing them leaders (42:3-4), and foreseeing strife over the office of overseer (44:1). It calls Paul and Cephas "apostles who had a good name" (47:4).

sections.h: 1 Clement: high priest, priests, Levites and layperson
sections.b: 1 Clement 40-41 sets out the ranks of Israel's worship: "the high priest has been given his own services. The priests have been assigned their own place. The Levites have their own ministries laid on them. The layperson is bound by the rules for laypeople" (1 Clement 40:5). The letter uses the order of the Temple to argue for order in the church, and calls Christ "the high priest and protector of our souls" (61:3; 64:1), but it never calls Christian ministers priests. The word for "layperson" here is the root of "laity."

1 Clement says the daily sacrifices and the offerings for vows, sin and guilt "are presented in Jerusalem alone," in front of the sanctuary, after the high priest checks the offering (1 Clement 41:2). The present tense has been used to date the letter before AD 70; Lightfoot judged that early date impossible and noted that Josephus and the Epistle of Barnabas describe the Temple in the present long after its fall.

1 Clement 43 retells Numbers 17 to show that God himself settles who may serve: Moses seals the twelve rods with the tribal leaders' rings, seals the tent's keys, and at morning "Aaron's rod was found not only sprouted but bearing fruit" (1 Clement 43:5). The seals and keys are details not found in Numbers.

sections.h: 1 Clement: Korah and the rebels at Corinth
sections.b: 1 Clement holds up Korah's band as the pattern of the Corinthian rebels: those "who rebelled against God's attendant Moses" hardened their hearts, and "they went down alive into Hades," and "death will be their shepherd" (1 Clement 51:3-4, joining Numbers 16:33 and Psalm 49:14). It also recalls the law's death penalty for those who broke the order of worship (41:3).

1 Clement calls Moses "a faithful attendant in the whole house" (1 Clement 43:1, from the Greek of Numbers 12:7, the verse of Hebrews 3:5), tells how he ended the quarrel over the priesthood (43:2-6), and praises his prayer after the golden calf, "Forgive this people their sin, or blot me out too from the book of the living" (53:4): "What great love! What perfection that cannot be outdone!" (53:5).

"Was Daniel thrown into the lions' pit by people who feared God?" (1 Clement 45:6). The Roman letter uses Daniel and the three young men to show that in Scripture the righteous were only ever persecuted by the wicked, never by holy men (45:3-8).

1 Clement names the three young men by their Hebrew names in Greek, "Ananias, Azarias and Misael," in the order of their song in the Greek Daniel, and asks whether they were "shut up in the fiery furnace by people who worshiped the Most High" (1 Clement 45:7).

sections.h: 1 Clement: "Take up the letter of the blessed Paul"
sections.b: About the end of the first century the Roman church told Corinth: "Take up the letter of the blessed Paul the apostle" (1 Clement 47:1). What it says Paul wrote, "about himself and Cephas and Apollos, because even then you had taken sides" (47:3), is 1 Corinthians 1:12 and 3:4-6. The letter also echoes 1 Corinthians 13 in its own praise of love (49:5).

The church that Paul founded at Corinth was, a generation or two later, "the solid and ancient church of the Corinthians," and it had removed its elders "because of one or two people" (1 Clement 47:6; 44:6). The Roman church asked the leaders of the revolt to leave (54:2), sent three messengers (63:3; 65:1), and urged the church to return to peace. About AD 170 the bishop of Corinth wrote that his church still read letters from Rome on the Lord's day (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

1 Clement 49-50 is a hymn to love written to the church that first heard 1 Corinthians 13: "Love joins us to God. Love lays a cover over a great number of sins. Love puts up with everything and is patient in everything ... Love has no split. Love does not rebel. Love does everything in harmony" (1 Clement 49:5). It ends with Christ, who "gave his blood for us ... his flesh for our flesh, and his soul for our souls" (49:6).

The Roman letter to Corinth holds up "the blessed Judith," who asked the elders to let her go out into the enemy camp "for love of her homeland and of her people under siege," and "the Lord handed Holofernes over by a woman's hand" (1 Clement 55:4-5). Clement uses her as a true example among women "made strong by the grace of God," without introducing the book as Scripture.

1 Clement calls Esther "perfect in faith" and says that "by her fasting and her humbling herself she pleaded with the all-seeing Master of the ages" (1 Clement 55:6). The fast is in Esther 4:16; the humbling points to her prayer in the Greek Additions to Esther (Addition C).

"Many handed themselves over into slavery, took the price paid for them, and fed others with it" (1 Clement 55:2). The Roman letter also speaks of Christians who gave themselves up to chains to ransom others. Lightfoot notes that "the ransom of slaves and the support of captives were regarded as a sacred duty by the early Christians generally."

1 Clement 59:2-61:3 is a long prayer of the Roman church. It praises God in Old Testament phrases (Isaiah 57:15; 1 Samuel 2:6-7; Deuteronomy 32:39), prays for the needy ("Lift the fallen to their feet. Make the sick well ... Ransom our prisoners," 59:4), asks forgiveness (60:1-2), and prays for rulers (61:1-2), ending "through the high priest and protector of our souls, Jesus Christ" (61:3). Its petitions match acts of God praised in Psalm 146 and in the Jewish Amidah's second blessing; Lightfoot traces its echoes in later liturgies such as the Apostolic Constitutions.

The Roman church prays: "You, Master, gave them the authority of kingship ... so that we ... would submit to them and in no way go against your will. Give them, Lord, health, peace, harmony and steadiness" (1 Clement 61:1). It asks to be made "obedient to your almighty and glorious name, and to our rulers and governors on the earth" (60:4), and that the rulers govern "in peace and gentleness, in a godly way" (61:2). The prayer carries out 1 Timothy 2:1-2 and Romans 13:1, written perhaps under Domitian.

sections.h: 1 Clement: true Scriptures "given through the Holy Spirit"
sections.b: 1 Clement calls the sacred Scriptures "the true ones, the ones given through the Holy Spirit," and says "nothing unjust or falsified is written in them" (1 Clement 45:2-3). It says Paul wrote to Corinth "truly led by the Spirit" (47:3) and that its own letter was written "through the Holy Spirit" (63:2), but it keeps "it is written" for the Old Testament. Eusebius says the letter was read publicly "in a great many churches" (Church History 3.16).

sections.h: 1 Clement 46:8: a saying of Jesus in Clement's form
sections.b: "Woe to that man! It would have been good for him if he had not been born, rather than trip up one of my chosen. It would have been better for him to have a millstone hung on him and be drowned in the sea, than to turn aside one of my chosen" (1 Clement 46:8). The saying joins Matthew 26:24 with Luke 17:2 (and Matthew 18:6; Mark 9:42) in a form that matches no Gospel; Codices Alexandrinus and Constantinopolitanus bring its end into line with the Gospels' "little ones."

"Why do we pull apart and tear to pieces the members of Christ? Why do we rebel against our own body ...?" (1 Clement 46:7). 1 Clement grounds the unity of the church in "one God ... one Christ, and one Spirit of grace" and "one calling" (46:6), calls the church "the flock of Christ" (44:3; 54:2; 57:2), and gives the gathered people a voice: elders are appointed "with the whole church agreeing" (44:3), and the departing rebel will "do what the people tell me" (54:2).
sections.refs: 1 Clement 44:3; 1 Clement 46:5-9; 1 Clement 54:2; 1 Clement 57:2; Ephesians 4:4-6; Romans 12:5

sections.b: The second half of 1 Clement keeps returning to its theme. The prayer asks God, "Grant harmony and peace to us and to everyone living on the earth" (1 Clement 60:4) and asks the same for the rulers (61:1-2). The noble rebel is to step aside, saying, "Only let Christ's flock live in peace with the elders who have been appointed" (54:2). The summary calls the Corinthians to live "in love and peace with steady forbearance" (62:2); the letter is called a plea "for peace and harmony" (63:2), its whole care "that you be at peace soon" (63:4), and the messengers are to report "the peace and harmony we pray for and long for" (65:1).
sections.refs: 1 Clement 54:2; 1 Clement 60:4; 1 Clement 61:1-2; 1 Clement 62:2; 1 Clement 63:2-4; 1 Clement 65:1

sections.h: 1 Clement: the church at Rome writes
sections.b: The letter ends, "The letter of the Romans to the Corinthians" (1 Clement 65:2), and speaks throughout as a church ("we"). Its messengers, Claudius Ephebus and Valerius Bito, bear names that Lightfoot thought "suggest some connexion with the imperial household" (65:1; compare Philippians 4:22). Its prayer for the rulers (61) and its report of Christians who sold themselves to feed others (55:2) show a Roman church at prayer and at work.

The great prayer of 1 Clement calls Jesus Christ God's "beloved servant" (Greek pais) three times (1 Clement 59:2-4), the word of the Greek Isaiah for God's servant (Isaiah 42:1; 52:13) and of the first church's prayers in Acts 4:27-30.

The letter that tradition gives to Clement never names him. It closes with three messengers, Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus (1 Clement 65:1), and the title "The letter of the Romans to the Corinthians" (65:2). Eusebius says Clement "wrote it in the name of the church of Rome to the church of Corinth" (Church History 3.16).

sections.h: 1 Clement: the harmony "handed down to us"
sections.b: 1 Clement speaks of "the harmony that was handed down to us so well and so justly" (1 Clement 51:2) and traces the church's leaders back through the apostles to Christ and God (42:1-4; 44:2). The letter grounds its appeal both in Scripture, quoted at length, and in what the apostles set in place; how the churches weigh these two is on the cards at 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and Matthew 15:3-9.
